metadata.title: A Framework for the Analysis of Student Well-Being in the PISA 2015 Study: Being 15 In 2015

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD framework paper does not report an empirical re-analysis of PISA 2015 microdata; instead, it specifies how PISA 2015 well-being constructs are operationalised through questionnaire instruments and indicators. As such, there is no described analytic subsample, no reported application of PISA student/school sampling weights, and no replicate-weight procedure (e.g., BRR/jackknife) documented in the text. For users who later conduct secondary analyses with PISA 2015 microdata, the appropriate approach is to apply PISA’s complex survey design weights (and replicate weights if variance estimation is required) when estimating population-representative statistics and uncertainty. Plausible values are not the focus here because the paper is primarily about measurement coverage and indicator mapping rather than achievement-score modelling.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper is a measurement and policy framework for analysing student well-being in PISA 2015, not an empirical predictive/causal analysis with a documented missing-data strategy. It does not specify a model-based estimation procedure that would require reporting how missing questionnaire responses were imputed or how PVs were combined. Therefore, missing-data handling is not applicable to the framework’s purpose and is not reported as an analytic step.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No analytic sample is defined because the paper does not conduct an empirical analysis of PISA 2015 microdata; it provides a comprehensive overview of the five well-being dimensions in PISA 2015 and maps the underlying indicators and questionnaire instruments (including student, school principal, and optional parent/education-career modules).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD Education Working Paper provides a conceptual and measurement framework for analysing student well-being in PISA 2015, organised into five dimensions: cognitive, psychological, physical, social, and material well-being. It specifies which indicators and questionnaire instruments (student self-reports, school principal reports, and optional parental/education-career modules) correspond to each dimension, and it discusses their theoretical and analytical value for education policy. The paper also clarifies that PISA remains primarily an assessment of learning outcomes, while the well-being module adds a multidimensional portrait of students’ experiences at age 15. Rather than estimating model effects, it synthesises prior evidence and identifies data gaps in the current questionnaire design, proposing how future PISA cycles could better distinguish inputs versus outcomes and strengthen policy relevance. No performance metrics, PV procedures, or missing-data/weighting methods are reported because the work is framework-focused rather than an empirical re-analysis.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse because the document is a framework/methodology paper rather than an empirical study: it does not report an analytic sample size, country-level Ns, PV handling, missing-data procedures, or any ML model training/evaluation. Consequently, fields that would normally capture predictive targets, performance metrics, and model-based findings are intentionally empty. The paper’s contribution is the mapping of PISA 2015 well-being dimensions to specific instruments and indicators, plus a roadmap for improving future measurement.
